newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Britain's Blair embraces family values.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair embraces family values.

text.p: British Labour Party leader Tony Blair called on Monday for a new social morality based on duty and family values and promised to lay the foundations of a modernised welfare state in his first five years in government.
"Liberty is not exercised in a moral vacuum," Blair, who is bidding to become Britain's first Labour prime minister in almost two decades, told the Commonwealth Press Union in Cape Town.

"A modern civic society, what I call the decent society, is a necessary part of our nation's continued progress. Such a society cannot be created unless it is based on certain social values, a shared social morality fit and right for today's world," he said.
"At the heart of everything New Labour stands for is the theme of rights and responsibilities. With every right we enjoy, we owe a duty, that is the most basic family value of all."

In a speech that made little reference to South Africa, the Commonwealth or to foreign policy, Blair embellished the family values theme already identified as a mantra of his bid to hang his hat in Downing Street.
"It is upon the values not only of the family, but of the extended family, that the decent society will be built.
"I don't mind admitting that I lament the loss of those decent British values. Nor do I believe it is impossible to rediscover the best of them. Politics has always been about values," he said.
Blair said family values and the moral standards of British society were likely to be central themes of the campaign for a general election due by early next year.
In his speech and at a news conference later, Blair denied that family values were synonymous with right wing values.
"But the absence of prejudice should not mean the absence of rules, of order, of stability. Let the social morality be based on reason, not bigotry," he said.

Blair repudiated aspects of his party's policy during the years of Conservative Party rule and said the past 45 years had seen a struggle to "strip away outdated ideology and the quasi-Marxist economic doctrines...of state control".
Freed from redundant ideological constraints, the party could now pursue a policy of hard-headed practicality married to idealism, he said.
"If at the end of the first five years of a new Labour government we have not put in place at least the foundation stones of a modernised welfare state, we will have failed," he said.
Blair said the Labour Party would push both the European Union and the Commonwealth, which links Britain and its former colonies, towards freer trade regimes.
He vowed to pursue fiscal responsibility in his search for a modern welfare state backed by its people.
"The days of tax, spend and borrow centre-left politics are over. No party competing for power should be anything other than fiscally prudent.
